# 🎓 Tutorial: the Northwest Pacific (FAO area 61) from zero to a report

📦 **Data**: [FAO Global Capture
Production](https://www.fao.org/fishery/collection/capture/en), release
**2026.1.0** (published by FAO on 2026-03-30; catches 1950–2024),
downloaded from
[Capture_2026.1.0.zip](https://www.fao.org/fishery/static/Data/Capture_2026.1.0.zip).
Licence [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
[`fao_data_info()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_info.md)
shows the release you use and how to cite it.

This tutorial walks through a complete assessment of one FAO major
fishing area, the **Northwest Pacific (FAO area 61)**, from an empty R
session to a finished report. It uses almost every function of the
package, in the order you would use them in your own work, and explains
**what each chart shows, how to read it and what it says about the
area**. If you have never used the package, read it from top to bottom
and run the code as you go; if you know the package, use the table of
contents to jump to the step you need.

Area 61 is a good teaching example: it is the largest fishing area of
the world by catch, it holds famous boom-and-bust species (the Pacific
sardine, the Alaska pollock), one country (China) takes most of the
catch, and a large part of the catch is not identified to species. Every
number in the text below is computed from the data when the page is
built, so it matches the charts.

| Step | What you do | Functions |
|----|----|----|
| [1](#prepare) | Prepare R, a project folder and the settings | [`fao_settings()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_settings.md), [`fao_font()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_font.md) |
| [2](#data) | Get the FAO data, know its version, save your own copy | [`check_fao_update()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/check_fao_update.md), [`download_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/download_fao_data.md), [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md), [`fao_data_info()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_info.md) |

**How the charts are explained.** Under each chart, “🔎 How to read it”
describes the axes, colours and lines, and “What it shows for area 61”
gives the result. Charts describe the **reported catch**: they say what
was landed and reported to FAO, not how many fish are in the sea. Keep
that in mind for every conclusion.

## 1. 🧰 Prepare

Install the package once, with all the packages it uses (see [🚀 Get
started](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/get-started.md)
for details), then load it at the start of every session:

``` r

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Linbojun99/faofishingreport", dependencies = TRUE)
```

``` r

library(faofishingreport)
```

**Work in a project folder.** Every function saves its charts and tables
in the *working directory* (the folder
[`getwd()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/getwd.html) returns). Create one
folder per assessment, e.g. with an RStudio project, or set it yourself:

``` r

dir.create("~/fao61", showWarnings = FALSE)
setwd("~/fao61")
getwd()
```

**Choose the settings once for the session** with
[`fao_settings()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_settings.md):
the language of the charts, their style and the output formats. Call it
without arguments to see the current settings.

``` r

fao_settings(lang = "en", theme = "classic", dpi = 100, pptx = FALSE)
```

| Setting | Here | What it does |
|----|----|----|
| `lang` | `"en"` | Chart text and names in English; `"zh"` Chinese; `"both"` both |
| `theme` | `"classic"` | Chart style (see [🎨 Customise](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/customise.md)) |
| `dpi` | `100` | Resolution of the PNG files (300 for print) |
| `pptx` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` also saves every chart as an editable PowerPoint file |

The chart font is chosen for your system
([`fao_font()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_font.md)
shows it): SimSun on Windows, Songti SC on macOS, Noto Serif CJK SC on
Linux, so that Chinese names display.

## 2. 💾 Get the data

### 2.1 Check for the newest FAO release

FAO publishes the Global Capture Production statistics once a year. The
package comes with a recent release;
[`check_fao_update()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/check_fao_update.md)
compares it with the newest one online, and
[`download_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/download_fao_data.md)
downloads and converts a release (about 6 MB, usually under a minute):

``` r

check_fao_update()     # newest release online vs. the data on your computer
download_fao_data()    # download the newest release (only when FAO publishes a new one)
```

### 2.2 Load the data and know which release you use

[`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md)
returns the newest release available on your computer (downloaded, or
else the one bundled with the package), one row per country, species
item, area and year:

``` r

fao <- load_fao_data()
dim(fao)
#> [1] 1024698       8
show_table(fao[fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. == "Pacific, Northwest" & fao$Year == 2024, ], n = 5)
```

|  | Country..Name. | ASFIS.species..Name. | FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. | Unit..Name. | Unit | Year | Production | Production.Type |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|---:|:---|
| 114028 | China | Elongate ilisha | Pacific, Northwest | Tonnes - live weight | TLW, Number | 2024 | 60,739 | actual |
| 114287 | China | Flathead grey mullet | Pacific, Northwest | Tonnes - live weight | TLW, Number | 2024 | 69,028 | actual |
| 114309 | China | So-iny (redlip) mullet | Pacific, Northwest | Tonnes - live weight | TLW, Number | 2024 | 98,932 | actual |
| 114344 | China | Groupers nei | Pacific, Northwest | Tonnes - live weight | TLW, Number | 2024 | 111,646 | actual |
| 114449 | China | Pacific sandlance | Pacific, Northwest | Tonnes - live weight | TLW, Number | 2024 | 81,171 | actual |

| Column | Meaning |
|----|----|
| `Country..Name.` | Reporting country (FAO English name) |
| `ASFIS.species..Name.` | FAO species item (a species, a genus, a family or a group such as “Marine fishes nei”, *nei* = not elsewhere included) |
| `FAO.major.fishing.area..Name.` | FAO major fishing area |
| `Year`, `Production` | Year and catch in tonnes live weight |
| `Production.Type` | How the value was obtained: reported by the country, estimated by FAO, … |

**Always record the release you used**: FAO revises past years in every
release, so a report must say which one it is based on.
[`fao_data_info()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_info.md)
gives the release, its dates, the download link and a citation:

``` r

info <- fao_data_info()
info
#> FAO Global Capture Production
#>   Release:   2026.1.0 (published by FAO on 2026-03-30)
#>   Years:     1950-2024
#>   File:      https://www.fao.org/fishery/static/Data/Capture_2026.1.0.zip
#>   Obtained:  bundled with faofishingreport, downloaded from FAO on 2026-10-10
#>   Licence:   CC BY 4.0 (https://www.fao.org/contact-us/terms/db-terms-of-use/en)
#>   Citation:  FAO. 2026. Global Capture Production 1950-2024, release 2026.1.0. In: Fisheries and Aquaculture [online]. Rome. [Cited 10 October 2026]. https://www.fao.org/fishery/collection/capture/en. Licence: CC BY 4.0.
```

### 2.3 Where the data are kept

Downloaded releases are kept in the data folder of the package,
[`fao_data_dir()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_dir.md),
and used again in every session. To share one folder between computers
or a team, set the environment variable `FAOFISHINGREPORT_DATA_DIR` in
`~/.Renviron` (see [💾 FAO
data](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/data.md)).
Your own copies of the data of an area can be saved like any R object:

``` r

fao_data_dir()
#> [1] "/home/runner/.local/share/R/faofishingreport"
area61_raw <- fao[fao$FAO.major.fishing.area..Name. == "Pacific, Northwest", ]
saveRDS(area61_raw, "area61_data.rds")                 # for R: readRDS("area61_data.rds")
write.csv(area61_raw, "area61_data.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")   # for Excel
```

## 3. 🌊 The catch of the area

[`fishing_area_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_data.md)
takes the name of an FAO major area, keeps its data, and draws the total
catch with its stages and the share of the area in the world marine
catch:

``` r

NWP <- fishing_area_data("Pacific, Northwest")
area61 <- NWP$area_data
```

![fishing_trend.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/fishing_trend.png`

![fishing_percentage.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/fishing_percentage.png`

**`fishing_trend.png`: total catch and its stages**

🔎 *How to read it.* The grey area is the yearly catch of the area
(million tonnes). The vertical dashed lines are **breakpoints**: years
in which the mean catch changes, found with the Bai-Perron test
([`strucchange::breakpoints()`](https://rdrr.io/pkg/strucchange/man/breakpoints.html));
a stage starts at each dashed line. The horizontal grey segments are the
mean catch of each stage.

*What it shows for area 61.* The catch rose from 4.5 million t in 1950
to a peak of 24.0 million t in 1997, and was 19.1 million t in 2024. The
test finds 5 stages: 1950–1960 (mean 7.1 million t); 1961–1972 (mean
11.1 million t); 1973–1983 (mean 17.4 million t); 1984–2000 (mean 22.4
million t); 2001–2024 (mean 20.3 million t). The growth of the
1950s–1980s, the high plateau of the late 1980s and 1990s and the lower,
steady catch since 2001 are the three things to explain in a report.

**`fishing_percentage.png`: share of the world marine catch**

🔎 *How to read it.* Each point is the catch of the area as a percentage
of the catch of all FAO marine areas in that year; the red line is the
mean of these shares. Inland waters are not counted.

*What it shows for area 61.* The area took between 20.4% and 31.2% of
the world marine catch, 26.3% on average, and 23.6% in 2024. A share
above its mean means the area grew faster (or declined more slowly) than
the rest of the world’s oceans.

`NWP` is a list: `NWP$area_data` (the data of the area, used by all the
next steps), `NWP$coefs_data` (the stages: first and last year and mean
catch) and `NWP$act_world_map` (the map data). Save it with
`saveRDS(NWP, "NWP.rds")` to continue later without recomputing.

## 4. 🐟 The main species

[`fishing_area_species()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_species.md)
ranks the species items by their catch (`rank_range = c(1, 10)`: the ten
largest), draws their catch over time and finds the stages of each:

``` r

sp <- fishing_area_species(area61, rank_range = c(1, 10))
```

![area_species.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/area/area_species.png`

![area_species_wrap.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/area/area_species_wrap.png`

**`area_species.png`: the main species together**, and
**`area_species_wrap.png`: one panel per species**

🔎 *How to read them.* The first chart puts the ten species items on one
scale, to compare their size. The second gives each species its own
panel and scale, so that small species are readable: the line is the
yearly catch, the dashed vertical lines and grey segments are the stages
of that species, the dashed slanted line is a linear trend, and the
percentage is the share of the species in the catch of the area over all
years.

*What it shows for area 61.* Over the last five years the largest items
were Marine fishes nei (2.94 million t a year), Alaska pollock(=Walleye
poll.) (2.09 million t a year), Pacific sardine (1.17 million t a year),
Largehead hairtail (0.99 million t a year), Pacific chub mackerel (0.97
million t a year). Three patterns stand out:

- **“Marine fishes nei” is the largest item.** It is not a species: it
  is fish that countries report without naming it. A large “nei” share
  limits what the species charts can say (see [data quality](#quality)).
- **Boom and bust.** The Pacific sardine went from almost nothing to a
  peak of 5.4 million t in 1988 and back to low catches within two
  decades, a well-known fluctuation of sardine populations with ocean
  conditions; it has risen again recently.
- **Alaska pollock** peaked in the late 1980s and declined in the 1990s,
  when the catch of the former USSR and of Japan fell.

Changing `rank_range` changes the species shown,
e.g. `rank_range = c(11, 20)` for the next ten. The lines in the panels
are smoothed only if `timeseries_analysis = FALSE`, which also removes
the stages.

## 5. 🌏 The main countries

[`fishing_area_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_country.md)
does the same for the countries, and adds a map of their catch:

``` r

co <- fishing_area_country(area61, rank_range = c(1, 8))
```

![area_country.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/area/area_country.png`

![area_country_wrap.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/area/area_country_wrap.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* As for the species: one panel per country with
its stages, trend and share of the catch over all years; the map colours
each country by its total catch in the area.

*What it shows for area 61.* Over the last five years, China (58.4%),
Russian Federation (19.2%), Japan (14.7%), Korea, Republic of (4.9%)
took most of the catch. **China** rose from 0.72 million t in 1950 to a
peak of 13.7 million t in 2015; **Japan**, the largest fishing country
of the area until 1991 (its peak: 10.0 million t in 1986; China has
caught more every year since 1992), caught 2.6 million t in 2024. The
panel of the **former USSR** ends in 1991 and the **Russian Federation**
starts in 1992: FAO keeps them as separate countries, so their stages
should be read together.

## 6. 🔍 One species, one country

### 6.1 Who catches a species: `species_country()`

``` r

pollock <- species_country(area61, "Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.)", rank_range = c(1, 5))
```

![Alaska_pollock\_\_Walleye_poll\_\_\_country_map.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/Alaska_pollock__Walleye_poll___country_map.png`

![Alaska_pollock\_\_Walleye_poll\_\_\_country_ranked_total.png](data:image/png;base64,)

![Alaska_pollock\_\_Walleye_poll\_\_\_country_ranked.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/species/Alaska_pollock__Walleye_poll___country_ranked.png`

![Alaska_pollock\_\_Walleye_poll\_\_\_country_ranked_wrap.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/species/Alaska_pollock__Walleye_poll___country_ranked_wrap.png`

![Alaska_pollock\_\_Walleye_poll\_\_\_country_pie_selected.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/species/Alaska_pollock__Walleye_poll___country_pie_selected.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* The charts break the catch of one species item
down by country: the ranked chart and the small multiples (one panel per
country, with stages), a pie chart of the countries by period and a map.
Species names must be written as in the FAO data
(`unique(area61$ASFIS.species..Name.)` lists them;
[`fao_translate()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_translate.md)
gives the Chinese names).

*What it shows for area 61.* The Alaska pollock of the Northwest Pacific
was caught mostly by the former USSR and then the Russian Federation,
Japan and the Republic of Korea; Japan’s catch peaked in the early
1970s, the USSR’s in the late 1980s, and Poland fished it in the late
1980s and the 1990s.

### 6.2 What a country catches: `country_species()` and `country_analysis()`

[`country_species()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_species.md)
breaks down the catch of one country in the area by species;
[`country_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_analysis.md)
looks at the same country in **all** FAO areas, to see where it fishes:

``` r

japan_61 <- country_species(area61, "Japan", rank_range = c(1, 10))
japan_all <- country_analysis("Japan", rank_range = c(1, 10))
```

🔎 *How to read them.* `Japan_species_*` charts: the species of Japan in
area 61. `Japananalysis_*` charts: the species of Japan in all areas,
its catch by area (`Japanyearly_area_production.png`, one line per area)
and a map of the areas where it fishes.

*What it shows.* Japan’s catch in area 61 was dominated by the Pacific
sardine in the 1980s; since then its main species have been the chub
mackerel, the sardine again, the Yesso scallop and the Japanese anchovy
(the pollock mattered mostly up to the 1990s). Area 61 has always been
by far Japan’s largest fishing area, and its catch there has fallen
steadily since the late 1980s.

## 7. 📈 Composition, stock status, trends and shifts

### 7.1 Species groups: `species_group_composition()`

``` r

groups <- species_group_composition(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_group_isscaap.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_group_isscaap.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_group_isscaap_share.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_group_isscaap_share.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* Species items are grouped into the ISSCAAP groups
of FAO (e.g. “Herrings, sardines, anchovies”, “Cods, hakes, haddocks”).
The stacked areas show the catch of each group, and the `_share` chart
its percentage of the catch; the largest groups are named, the others
are “Other groups”.

*What it shows for area 61.* The cods, hakes and haddocks (mostly
pollock) and the herrings, sardines and anchovies (mostly sardine and
anchovy) took the largest shares in the 1980s; since the 2000s the catch
is spread over more groups, with a larger share of miscellaneous coastal
and pelagic fishes, squids and shrimps.

### 7.2 Stock status plots: `stock_status()`

``` r

status <- stock_status(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_stock_status_stocks.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_stock_status_stocks.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_stock_status_catch.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_stock_status_catch.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* Each “stock” is the catch series of one species
item in the area. Every year, a stock is classed by its catch relative
to its own peak (Kleisner et al. 2013): **developing** (before the peak,
below half of it), **exploited** (above half of the peak),
**over-exploited** (after the peak, 10–50% of it), **collapsed** (after
the peak, below 10%) and **rebuilding** (back to 10–50% after a
collapse). The `_stocks` chart counts stocks, the `_catch` chart weights
them by their catch.

*What it shows for area 61.* Of the 217 stocks, in 2024 41.5% were
collapsed and 24.9% over-exploited by number. Weighted by catch the
picture is different: the collapsed stocks took only 0.5% of the catch,
because they are small, while the over-exploited stocks took 36.7% and
the exploited ones 51.7%. Many small stocks have fallen far below their
peaks, and a large part of the catch now comes from stocks below half of
theirs.

**What not to conclude.** A stock status plot uses catch only. A fall in
catch can come from fewer fish, but also from less fishing, management,
markets or a change in reporting (e.g. a species reported as “nei”). Use
it to ask questions, not as a stock assessment; `smooth = TRUE` classes
the 3-year running mean, which reduces the effect of single bad years.

### 7.3 Peak and trend of each species: `peak_trend()`

``` r

pt <- peak_trend(area61)
show_table(pt[, c("name", "peak_year", "pct_of_peak", "growth_pct_per_year", "trend")], n = 10)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_peak_trend_species.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_peak_trend_species.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* For each of the main species: the year of its peak
catch, the catch of the last year as a percentage of that peak, the mean
yearly growth over the last ten years and the Mann-Kendall test of that
trend (“up”, “down” or “none” at *P* \< 0.05).

### 7.4 Synchronous shifts: `regime_shift()`

``` r

shifts <- regime_shift(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_regime_shift.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_regime_shift.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_regime_shift_species.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_regime_shift_species.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* The breakpoints of each main species are found as
in step 4; the bar chart counts, for every year, how many species
changed their mean catch in that year. Years when many species change
together point to a common cause: the ocean (a regime shift), a change
of management, or a change of reporting.

*What it shows for area 61.* The years with the most simultaneous
breakpoints are 2014 (8 species), 1992 (5 species), 2003 (5 species).

### 7.5 All FAO areas compared: `area_overview()`

``` r
overview <- area_overview()
```

![marine_areas_peak_trend_area.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/marine_areas_peak_trend_area.png`

![marine_areas_catch.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/marine_areas_catch.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* The catch of every FAO marine area over time, and
their peak year and recent trend. It places area 61 among the others: it
is the area with the largest catch.

## 8. 🔍 Data quality, diversity and fleets

### 8.1 How good are the data? `data_quality()`

``` r

quality <- data_quality(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_data_quality_status_share.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_data_quality_status_share.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_data_quality_taxon_share.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_data_quality_taxon_share.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* `_taxon_share`: the share of the catch identified
to species, genus, family, or only to order or higher (e.g. “Marine
fishes nei”). `_status_share`: the share reported officially by
countries and the share estimated by FAO or the country.

*What it shows for area 61.* In 2024, 58.3% of the catch was identified
to species and 25.3% only to order or higher. The species charts above
therefore describe only part of the catch, and changes in identification
can look like changes in species. This is one of the main limitations to
state in a report on area 61.

### 8.2 Diversity and concentration: `diversity_concentration()`

``` r

div <- diversity_concentration(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_diversity.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_diversity.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* Seven indicators, one per panel: the number of
species items and of countries reporting, the Shannon diversity of the
species, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of the species and of the
countries, and the share of the five largest species and countries. The
HHI goes from near 0 (catch spread over many) to 10 000 (one takes all);
above 2 500 is “highly concentrated”.

*What it shows for area 61.* In 2024, 136 species items and 9 countries
reported catch; the HHI of the countries was 4136, highly concentrated,
because of China’s share, while the HHI of the species (569) shows a
catch spread over many species.

### 8.3 Who fishes: `country_group_summary()` and `coastal_distant()`

``` r

income <- country_group_summary(area61)
fleets <- coastal_distant(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_country_income.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_country_income.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_country_income_share.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_country_income_share.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_coastal_distant.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_coastal_distant.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* `country_income`: the catch by World Bank income
group of the countries. `coastal_distant`: the catch of **coastal
countries** (whose territory borders the area) and of **distant-water
countries**, from the FAO area boundaries and country outlines.

*What it shows for area 61.* Nearly all the catch is taken by coastal
countries: the countries around the Northwest Pacific fish their own
waters, and distant-water catch was only a small share in the 1980s and
1990s.

## 9. 🔬 Methods from the literature

These analyses follow published methods; [🔬 Shocks, collapses,
synchrony and
fleets](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/literature-analyses.md)
explains each in detail.

### 9.1 Catch shocks: `catch_shocks()`

``` r

shocks_country <- catch_shocks(area61)
shocks_species <- catch_shocks(area61, by = "species", label = "area61_species")
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_shocks.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_shocks.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_shocks_series.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_shocks_series.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_shocks_by_continent.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_shocks_by_continent.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_shocks_by_country.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_shocks_by_country.png`

![area61_species_shocks.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/area61_species_shocks.png`

![area61_species_shocks_series.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/area61_species_shocks_series.png`

![area61_species_shocks_by_species.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/area61_species_shocks_by_species.png`

![area61_species_shocks_by_species_group.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/area61_species_shocks_by_species_group.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* A **shock** is a year in which the catch of a
series fell far below what its recent years predicted (Cottrell et
al. 2019). The bar chart gives the percentage of series with a shock in
each year; `_series` shows the series with their shocks, `_by_country` /
`_by_continent` count them by group.

*What it shows for area 61.* By country (`by = c("country", "area")`,
the default), area 61 has only 9 series, so each shock is a large
percentage and the chart is coarse. By species there are 235 series and
75 shocks, a more informative picture for one area. **Choose the series
to fit the question**: countries for national food supply, species for
ecology.

### 9.2 Fishery collapses: `collapse_analysis()`

``` r

set.seed(1)   # the comparison with random series uses random numbers
collapses <- collapse_analysis(area61)
show_table(collapses$summary)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_collapse_mullon2005.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_collapse_mullon2005.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_collapse_mullon2005_types.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_collapse_mullon2005_types.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_collapse_mullon2005_by_group.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_collapse_mullon2005_by_group.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* A series (one species by one country) has
**collapsed** when, after its maximum, its catch stays below a tenth of
the maximum for four years (Mullon et al. 2005). The bars count
collapses by year and by the shape of the decline before them (plateau,
smooth or erratic). The function repeats the analysis on random series
without trend, because random ups and downs alone produce some
“collapses” (Wilberg and Miller 2007): only the excess over that null
model is informative.

### 9.3 Synchrony and the portfolio effect: `catch_synchrony()`

``` r

sync <- catch_synchrony(area61)
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_synchrony_species.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_synchrony_species.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_synchrony_species_cv.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_synchrony_species_cv.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_synchrony_species_correlation.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_synchrony_species_correlation.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* `_cv`: the coefficient of variation (year-to-year
variability) of each species and, in red, of the total catch.
`_correlation`: how the species vary together. The synchrony index φ is
0 when species compensate each other and 1 when they rise and fall
together (Loreau and de Mazancourt 2008).

*What it shows for area 61.* φ = 0.2: the total catch varies (CV 0.24)
much less than its species (mean CV 0.6): the species are on average
147% more variable than their total. This **portfolio effect** means
that when one species declines, others take its place. Among the main
species in the chart, the Pacific sardine is by far the most variable.

### 9.4 Pelagic to demersal ratio: `pelagic_demersal()`

``` r

pd <- pelagic_demersal(area61)
show_table(pd$decades[, c("period", "pd_mean", "pd_min", "pd_max")])
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_pelagic_demersal_ratio.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_pelagic_demersal_ratio.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_pelagic_demersal.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_pelagic_demersal.png`

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_pelagic_demersal_share.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_pelagic_demersal_share.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* P/D is the catch of small pelagic fishes divided
by the catch of demersal fishes and crustaceans (Caddy 1993; de Leiva
Moreno et al. 2000), on a log scale; the dashed line is P/D = 1. In
semi-enclosed seas a rising P/D has been linked to nutrient enrichment;
in open areas like area 61 it mostly follows the big swings of the small
pelagic fishes.

*What it shows for area 61.* P/D stayed below 1; its highest values came
in the 1980s, the decade of the sardine boom, and it has risen again
since the 2010s.

### 9.5 A distant-water fleet: `distant_water_profile()`

``` r

china_dw <- distant_water_profile("China")
```

![China_distant_water.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/China_distant_water.png`

![China_distant_water_share.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/China_distant_water_share.png`

![China_distant_water_areas.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/China_distant_water_areas.png`

![China_distant_water_n_areas.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/China_distant_water_n_areas.png`

![China_distant_water_timeline.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/China_distant_water_timeline.png`

🔎 *How to read them.* The catch of one country in the FAO areas it
borders (“adjacent”) and in the others (“distant-water”), the share of
distant-water catch, the number of areas fished each year and when it
entered each area (Swartz et al. 2010).

*What it shows.* Area 61 is China’s only adjacent area and gives most of
its catch. China’s distant-water catch grew from the late 1990s to 0.73
million t in 2024 (6.1% of its catch), in 12 distant FAO areas. FAO
notes that in 2022 China gave species and areas only for the catch
landed in China, and part of its distant-water catch was entered as
“Marine fishes nei” in area 61 (FAO 2024): recent distant-water catch is
partly counted in area 61, which also adds to the “nei” share seen in
[data quality](#quality).

## 10. 🌡️ Species traits and temperature

### 10.1 FishBase traits: `fishbase_match()`

``` r

traits <- fishbase_match(area61, version = "builtin")
show_table(traits[, c("species_en", "catch_pct", "match_type", "trophic_level", "temp_pref_mean")], n = 8)
```

| species_en | catch_pct | match_type | trophic_level | temp_pref_mean |
|:---|---:|:---|---:|---:|
| Marine fishes nei | 16.58 | not matched | NA | NA |
| Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.) | 12.84 | exact | 3.57 | 1.6 |
| Pacific sardine | 6.73 | exact | 2.84 | 17.9 |
| Pacific chub mackerel | 6.08 | exact | 3.38 | 20.7 |
| Largehead hairtail | 4.64 | exact | 4.42 | 15.2 |
| Japanese anchovy | 4.55 | exact | 3.14 | 18.4 |
| Marine molluscs nei | 2.71 | phylum | 3.01 | NA |
| Japanese flying squid | 2.26 | exact | 4.28 | 18.3 |

🔎 *How to read it.* Each FAO species item is matched to FishBase or
SeaLifeBase by published rules (exact name, synonym, WoRMS, the mean of
a higher taxon); `match_type` says which rule was used and each row has
links to check it. `version = "builtin"` uses the table bundled with the
package, so it works offline. Matches are first guesses: check the main
ones with the links (see [🐠
FishBase](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/fishbase.md)).

### 10.2 Sea surface temperature and the mean temperature of the catch

``` r

sst61 <- fao_area_sst("Pacific, Northwest")
mtc <- mean_temperature_catch(area61, version = "builtin")
show_table(mtc$trend[, c("period_start", "period_end", "mtc_slope_per_decade", "trend", "sst_slope_per_decade", "cor_mtc_sst")])
```

![Pacific\_\_Northwest_mtc.png](data:image/png;base64,)

`figures/png/summary/Pacific__Northwest_mtc.png`

🔎 *How to read it.* The **mean temperature of the catch** (MTC, red) is
the average preferred temperature of the species caught, weighted by
their catch (Cheung et al. 2013); the blue line is the sea surface
temperature (SST) of the area and the light band its range within the
area. The lower panel is the share of the catch with a known preferred
temperature; years below 50% are faded. A rising MTC means warm-water
species take a larger share of the catch.

*What it shows for area 61.* The MTC fell to a low of 10.7 °C in 1973,
when the cold-water Alaska pollock (preferred temperature 1.6 °C) took a
growing share of the catch; it rose to 15.7 °C in 2006 and has fallen
again since, to 13.8 °C in 2024. Species of warmer waters such as the
Pacific sardine (17.9 °C) move it up and down as their catches boom and
decline. The SST of the area warmed by 0.11 °C per decade over
1950–2024. The MTC of area 61 therefore reflects the fishery and its
target species as much as the ocean: read it with the species charts.

## 11. 📉 Stock assessment of the main species

[`cmsy_area()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/cmsy_area.md)
runs the CMSY++ catch-only stock assessment (Froese et al. 2023) for the
species with the largest catch. It needs the JAGS program once
([`cmsy_setup()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/cmsy_setup.md),
see [📉
CMSY++](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/cmsy.md))
and takes a few minutes; the charts below were made beforehand with the
same code.

``` r

cmsy_setup()                                            # once: JAGS and the R packages
nwp_cmsy <- cmsy_area("Pacific, Northwest", top = 10)   # the ten main species
nwp_cmsy$summary                                        # B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy, MSY, status
```

![kobe_all.png](data:image/png;base64,)

🔎 *How to read the Kobe plot.* Each circle is one stock in its last
year: its biomass relative to the biomass that gives the maximum
sustainable yield (B/Bmsy, horizontal) and its fishing pressure relative
to the one that gives it (F/Fmsy, vertical); the size is the catch.
Green (bottom right): healthy; red (top left): overfished and still
overfishing; orange and yellow: one of the two. The dashed line at
B/Bmsy = 0.8 separates “maximally sustainably fished” from “overfished”
in the FAO classes for catch-only results.

*What it shows for area 61.* 4 of the 10 stocks assessed were below 0.8
Bmsy in their last year.

| Stock | species | B_Bmsy | F_Fmsy | MSY | status |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| ALK_61 | Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.) | 0.66 | 1.02 | 3,328,272 | overfished |
| CHP_61 | Pacific sardine | 0.37 | 1.39 | 3,646,645 | overfished |
| MAS_61 | Pacific chub mackerel | 0.68 | 1.04 | 1,274,729 | overfished |
| LHT_61 | Largehead hairtail | 0.89 | 1.06 | 1,066,351 | maximally sustainably fished |
| JAN_61 | Japanese anchovy | 0.75 | 0.85 | 1,388,775 | overfished |
| HEP_61 | Pacific herring | 1.05 | 1.15 | 421,349 | maximally sustainably fished |
| AKS_61 | Akiami paste shrimp | 0.89 | 0.74 | 539,645 | maximally sustainably fished |
| GAZ_61 | Gazami crab | 1.04 | 0.97 | 500,590 | maximally sustainably fished |
| CRY_61 | Yellow croaker | 0.86 | 0.94 | 363,117 | maximally sustainably fished |
| DPC_61 | Daggertooth pike conger | 1.01 | 0.96 | 351,455 | maximally sustainably fished |

![overview.png](data:image/png;base64,)

🔎 *How to read it.* One row per stock: its B/Bmsy in the last year with
the 95% confidence limits (the bar), coloured by status. A long bar
means the data could not pin the stock size down.

![status_time.png](data:image/png;base64,)

🔎 *How to read it.* The share of the assessed stocks in each status
class, year by year. It shows whether the stocks of the area moved
together, e.g. all declining in the same years.

![management_first.png](data:image/png;base64,)

🔎 *How to read it.* The “management” chart of the largest stock (Alaska
pollock(=Walleye poll.)): the catch with the MSY (top left), the fishing
pressure F/Fmsy (top right), the biomass B/Bmsy with the lines at Bmsy
and 0.8 Bmsy (bottom left), and the path of the stock through the Kobe
plot (bottom right). Shaded bands are the 95% limits. See [📉
CMSY++](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/cmsy.md)
for all CMSY++ charts.

FAO capture statistics have no abundance index, so these are
**catch-only** assessments driven largely by their priors: indicative
only, never a replacement for a full stock assessment. The CMSY++ code
is that of its authors (<https://github.com/SISTA16/cmsyPlusPlus>); see
the disclaimer in [📉
CMSY++](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/cmsy.md).

## 12. 📝 The report in Word, LaTeX and PDF

[`fao_report()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_report.md)
runs the analyses of the area and writes the whole assessment as a
report: cover, abstract, data and methods, results with charts and
tables, conclusions, references and appendix. Here a Word report in
English, with the catch shocks and the mean temperature of the catch
added to the default sections:

``` r

report <- fao_report(61, lang = "en", shocks = TRUE, mtc = TRUE)
report
#> FAO report: /tmp/RtmpCRKciG/faofishingreport_site_1ea8e7585863c/reports/FAO61_report_en.docx
#> Sections: total, species, countries, groups, status, quality, diversity, fleets, shocks, mtc
#>   $main_species           main species of the last five years (10 rows)
#>   $main_countries         main fishing countries of the last five years (9 rows)
#>   $mtc_species            species of the mean temperature of the catch, with FishBase matches (284 rows)
#>   $analyses               results of the analyses: total, species, countries, groups, status, quality, diversity, fleets, shocks, mtc
```

The headings of the Word file:

``` r

doc <- officer::docx_summary(officer::read_docx(report$file[["docx"]]))
headings <- doc$text[doc$style_name %in% c("FAO Heading 1", "FAO Heading 2")]
headings
#>  [1] "1 Data and methods"                          
#>  [2] "1.1 Data sources"                            
#>  [3] "1.2 Methods"                                 
#>  [4] "2 Results and conclusions"                   
#>  [5] "2.1 Catch trends and stages"                 
#>  [6] "2.2 Main species"                            
#>  [7] "2.3 Main fishing countries"                  
#>  [8] "2.4 Composition by species group"            
#>  [9] "2.5 Stock status"                            
#> [10] "2.6 Data quality"                            
#> [11] "2.7 Diversity and concentration of the catch"
#> [12] "2.8 Coastal and distant-water fleets"        
#> [13] "2.9 Catch shocks"                            
#> [14] "2.10 Mean temperature of the catch"          
#> [15] "2.11 Conclusions"                            
#> [16] "References"                                  
#> [17] "Appendix"
```

The same report as LaTeX and PDF, in Chinese, with CMSY++ (reusing the
results of step 11 so CMSY++ does not run again):

``` r

fao_report(61, lang = "zh", format = c("docx", "latex", "pdf"), shocks = TRUE, mtc = TRUE,
           cmsy = nwp_cmsy)
```

| File | What it is |
|----|----|
| `reports/FAO61_report_en.docx` | The Word report, to edit and complete |
| `reports/FAO61_report_zh.tex` and `reports/FAO61_report_zh_figures/` | The LaTeX source and its figures |
| `reports/FAO61_report_zh.pdf` | The PDF (needs XeLaTeX, e.g. through tinytex) |

The report is a **first draft**: the text is written from templates
filled with the results. Read it, complete the grey “To be completed”
notes (other data sources, discussion, other references) and check every
conclusion against the charts above. See [📝 Assessment
report](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/report.md)
for every option.

## 13. 🗂️ Where everything is saved and how to get it back

Every function writes into the working directory:

| Folder | What | Written by |
|----|----|----|
| `figures/png/` | `fishing_trend.png`, `fishing_percentage.png` | [`fishing_area_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_data.md) |
| `figures/png/area/` | `area_species*.png`, `area_country*.png` | [`fishing_area_species()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_species.md), [`fishing_area_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_country.md) |
| `figures/png/` | `area_country_map.png`, `<species>_country_map.png` | maps of [`fishing_area_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_country.md), [`species_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/species_country.md) |
| `figures/png/species/` | `<species>_country_*.png` | [`species_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/species_country.md) |
| `figures/png/country/` | `<country>_species_*.png`, `<country>analysis_*.png`, `<country>yearly_area_production*.png` | [`country_species()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_species.md), [`country_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_analysis.md) |
| `figures/png/summary/` | `<label>_<analysis>*.png`, e.g. `Pacific__Northwest_stock_status_stocks.png` | the summary and literature analyses |
| `figures/pptx/...` | The same charts as PowerPoint files | when `pptx = TRUE` |
| `tables/` | CSV tables (UTF-8, open in Excel) | every function with `table = TRUE` |
| `reports/` | The reports, and `reports/cmsy/` with the CMSY++ results | [`fao_report()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_report.md) |
| `cmsy_areas/` | The CMSY++ runs, charts and tables of each area | [`cmsy_area()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/cmsy_area.md) |


**Getting results back.** Every function also returns its results to R
(assign them, as above). To continue another day, save them and read
them back, or read the CSV tables:

``` r

saveRDS(list(NWP = NWP, status = status, mtc = mtc), "area61_results.rds")
results <- readRDS("area61_results.rds")
names(results)
#> [1] "NWP"    "status" "mtc"
head(read.csv("tables/Pacific__Northwest_stock_status_stocks.csv"), 3)
#>                     species_name                     species_en first_year
#> 1                Pacific sardine                Pacific sardine       1950
#> 2 Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.) Alaska pollock(=Walleye poll.)       1950
#> 3          Pacific chub mackerel          Pacific chub mackerel       1950
#>   peak_year peak_tonnes last_year_tonnes pct_of_peak status_last_year
#> 1      1988     5428922        1356038.9    24.97805       Rebuilding
#> 2      1986     5153770        2139094.1    41.50542   Over-exploited
#> 3      1978     2238781         866611.1    38.70906   Over-exploited
```

When FAO publishes a new release, run
[`download_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/download_fao_data.md)
and the same code again: every chart, table and number is recomputed
from the new data, and
[`fao_data_info()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_info.md)
gives the new citation.

## 14. 🎨 Make it yours

The same analyses in Chinese or bilingual charts, another style or map
projection:

``` r

fao_settings(lang = "zh")                  # Chinese charts and names
fao_settings(lang = "both")                # Chinese and English on the same chart
fao_settings(theme = "minimal", palette = "npg", map_projection = "robinson", map_center = 180)
fao_settings(reset = TRUE)                 # back to the defaults
```

See [🎨 Customise charts and
maps](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/articles/customise.md)
for all settings.

## ✅ Summary

| Step | Function | Main output |
|----|----|----|
| Data | [`load_fao_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/load_fao_data.md), [`fao_data_info()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_data_info.md) | The data and the release to cite |
| Area | [`fishing_area_data()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_data.md) | Total catch, stages, share of the world |
| Species, countries | [`fishing_area_species()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_species.md), [`fishing_area_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishing_area_country.md), [`species_country()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/species_country.md), [`country_species()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_species.md), [`country_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_analysis.md) | Who catches what, and its stages |
| Status | [`species_group_composition()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/species_group_composition.md), [`stock_status()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/stock_status.md), [`peak_trend()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/peak_trend.md), [`regime_shift()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/regime_shift.md), [`area_overview()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/area_overview.md) | Composition, status, trends, shifts |
| Quality, fleets | [`data_quality()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/data_quality.md), [`diversity_concentration()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/diversity_concentration.md), [`country_group_summary()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/country_group_summary.md), [`coastal_distant()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/coastal_distant.md) | How reliable and how concentrated |
| Literature | [`catch_shocks()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_shocks.md), [`collapse_analysis()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/collapse_analysis.md), [`catch_synchrony()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/catch_synchrony.md), [`pelagic_demersal()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/pelagic_demersal.md), [`distant_water_profile()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/distant_water_profile.md) | Shocks, collapses, synchrony, P/D, fleets |
| Temperature | [`fishbase_match()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fishbase_match.md), [`fao_area_sst()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_area_sst.md), [`mean_temperature_catch()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/mean_temperature_catch.md) | Traits, SST, MTC |
| Assessment | [`cmsy_area()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/cmsy_area.md) | B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy, MSY |
| Report | [`fao_report()`](https://linbojun99.github.io/faofishingreport/reference/fao_report.md) | Word, LaTeX, PDF |
